expectedText:
VOLUNTEER EMERGENCY RESPONDER LEAVE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes two related but distinct California job protections for an employee who serves as a volunteer firefighter, a reserve peace officer, or emergency rescue personnel: (1) the right under Labor Code § 230.3 not to be discharged or discriminated against for taking time off to perform actual emergency duty, which applies regardless of employer size but does not apply to certain public safety or emergency medical services employers; and (2) the separate right under Labor Code § 230.4, available only at employers with 50 or more employees, to take up to 14 days per calendar year of leave for fire, law enforcement, or emergency rescue training. It does not cover unrelated leave topics such as jury duty, witness leave, or military leave under USERRA, which are addressed in separate information sheets.

WHO IS COVERED: VOLUNTEER FIREFIGHTER, EMERGENCY RESCUE PERSONNEL, HEALTH CARE PROVIDER
Labor Code § 230.3 protects an employee who serves as a "volunteer firefighter," a "reserve peace officer," or "emergency rescue personnel." "Volunteer firefighter" has the same meaning as "volunteer" in Government Code § 50952, which defines it as a person registered as a volunteer member of a regularly organized fire department. "Emergency rescue personnel" is defined broadly to include any officer, employee, or member of a federal, state, or local fire department or firefighting agency, a sheriff's department, a police department, a private fire department, or a state-sponsored disaster medical response entity — whether that person is a volunteer, partly paid, or fully paid — while actually engaged in providing emergency services as defined by Health & Safety Code § 1799.107. A "health care provider" is any person licensed or certified under Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code, or under the Osteopathic Initiative Act or the Chiropractic Initiative Act.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(d) (1) For purposes of this section, “volunteer firefighter” shall have the same meaning as the term “volunteer” in Section 50952 of the Government Code.(2) For purposes of this section, “emergency rescue personnel” means any person who is an officer, employee, or member of a fire department or fire protection or firefighting agency of the federal government, the State of California, a city, county, city and county, district, or other public or municipal corporation or political subdivision of this state, or of a sheriff’s department, police department, or a private fire department, or of a disaster medical response entity sponsored or requested by this state, whether that person is a volunteer or partly paid or fully paid, while he or she is actually engaged in providing emergency services as defined by Section 1799.107 of the Health and Safety Code."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3(d)(1)-(2), definitions of volunteer firefighter and emergency rescue personnel (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.3.)
  "(p) “Volunteer” means a person registered as a volunteer member of a regularly organized fire department as defined in subdivision (k)."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 50952 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 50952(p), definition of "volunteer" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=50952.)
  Known gap: The definition of "emergency rescue personnel" cross-references Health & Safety Code § 1799.107 for the meaning of "emergency services," and this document did not independently fetch and verify the text of that section — so it does not state, beyond the statutory label, exactly which activities count as "actually engaged in providing emergency services." The definition covers a person only while actually engaged in providing those emergency services, meaning off-duty volunteer-department membership without an active emergency response or training event is not, by this text alone, established as covered conduct under § 230.3(a). Both the "volunteer firefighter" and "emergency rescue personnel" definitions were verified from the same fetched-and-confirmed copy of Labor Code § 230.3(d); the Government Code § 50952 definition was independently fetched and confirmed from a separate source page.

EMERGENCY DUTY TIME-OFF NOTICE
Jordan Lee provides this notice to Acme, Inc. of time off taken or requested under Labor Code § 230.3 to perform emergency duty for Cal Fire, Sonoma County Volunteer Fire Department, in the role checked below.

☐ Volunteer firefighter
☐ Reserve peace officer
☐ Emergency rescue personnel

Dates of emergency duty: September 8, 2026 through September 9, 2026
Nature of the emergency duty performed (brief description): _______________________________________________
If Jordan Lee is a health care provider, date this employee notified Acme, Inc. of their designation as emergency rescue personnel: _______________
Date this notice is given to Acme, Inc.: _______________

PROTECTION FROM DISCHARGE OR DISCRIMINATION FOR EMERGENCY DUTY
Under Labor Code § 230.3(a), an employer shall not discharge or in any manner discriminate against an employee for taking time off to perform emergency duty as a volunteer firefighter, a reserve peace officer, or emergency rescue personnel. This protection applies regardless of the employer's size, unlike the training-leave right described elsewhere in this document, which applies only at employers with 50 or more employees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "230.3. (a) An employer shall not discharge or in any manner discriminate against an employee for taking time off to perform emergency duty as a volunteer firefighter, a reserve peace officer, or emergency rescue personnel."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3(a), anti-discrimination protection for emergency duty absence (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.3.)
  Known gap: The statute's text does not itself state any cap on the number of days of emergency-duty time off that is protected, in contrast to the 14-day annual cap the same statutory scheme places on training leave under § 230.4(a); this document does not assert that emergency-duty absences are protected without any limit, only that the verified text of § 230.3(a) does not state a numerical limit. The statute is also silent on whether time off under this subdivision must be paid by the employer, and this document does not assert that it is.

NOTICE DUTY FOR EMPLOYEES WHO ARE HEALTH CARE PROVIDERS
An employee who is a health care provider must notify their employer at the time the employee becomes designated as emergency rescue personnel, and again when the employee is notified that they will be deployed as a result of that designation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(2) An employee who is a health care provider shall notify his or her employer at the time the employee becomes designated as emergency rescue personnel and when the employee is notified that he or she will be deployed as a result of that designation."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3(c)(2), health care provider notice duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.3.)
  Known gap: This notice duty, verified from Labor Code § 230.3(c)(2), applies by its own terms only to an employee who meets the statute's separate definition of "health care provider" (licensed or certified under Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code, or under the Osteopathic Initiative Act or the Chiropractic Initiative Act); this document does not assert that any other volunteer firefighter, reserve peace officer, or emergency rescue personnel has an equivalent statutory notice duty, because the verified text imposes this specific duty only on the health-care-provider subset.

EXCEPTION FOR CERTAIN PUBLIC SAFETY AND EMERGENCY MEDICAL SERVICES EMPLOYERS
The protections in Labor Code § 230.3(a) and (b) do not apply to any public safety agency or provider of emergency medical services if, as determined by that employer, the employee's absence would hinder the availability of public safety or emergency medical services.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(c) (1) Subdivisions (a) and (b) of this section shall not apply to any public safety agency or provider of emergency medical services if, as determined by the employer, the employee’s absence would hinder the availability of public safety or emergency medical services."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3(c)(1), exception for certain public safety and EMS employers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.3.)
  Known gap: This exception applies only when the employer itself is a public safety agency or an emergency medical services provider, and the statute leaves the hindrance determination to that employer's own judgment ("as determined by the employer") without stating any external standard, review process, or documentation requirement this document could verify; this document does not describe how, if at all, an employee could challenge that employer determination, because the verified statutory text does not itself specify one.

REMEDIES FOR VIOLATION OF THE EMERGENCY DUTY PROTECTION
An employee who is discharged, threatened with discharge, demoted, suspended, or otherwise discriminated against in the terms and conditions of employment because the employee took time off to perform emergency duty as a volunteer firefighter, a reserve peace officer, or emergency rescue personnel is entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the employer's acts. An employer who willfully refuses to rehire, promote, or otherwise restore an employee or former employee who has been determined eligible for rehiring or promotion through a grievance procedure, arbitration, or hearing authorized by law is guilty of a misdemeanor.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(b) An employee who is discharged, threatened with discharge, demoted, suspended, or in any other manner discriminated against in the terms and conditions of employment by his or her employer because the employee has taken time off to perform emergency duty as a volunteer firefighter, a reserve peace officer, or emergency rescue personnel shall be entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the acts of the employer. Any employer who willfully refuses to rehire, promote, or otherwise restore an employee or former employee who has been determined to be eligible for rehiring or promotion by a grievance procedure, arbitration, or hearing authorized by law, is guilty of a misdemeanor."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3(b), reinstatement, reimbursement, and misdemeanor penalty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.3.)
  Known gap: This clause, verified from Labor Code § 230.3(b), does not itself describe the procedural mechanism (such as a Labor Commissioner complaint) by which an employee obtains this reinstatement and reimbursement; § 230.3 does not contain an explicit cross-reference to Labor Code § 98.7 the way § 230.4(c) does for the separate training-leave right, so this document does not assert that the § 98.7 complaint procedure described elsewhere in this document applies to a § 230.3 emergency-duty violation, only that it applies to a § 230.4 training-leave violation, where the statute expressly says so.

FIRE, LAW ENFORCEMENT, OR EMERGENCY RESCUE TRAINING LEAVE REQUEST
Jordan Lee requests leave from Acme, Inc. under Labor Code § 230.4 to attend fire, law enforcement, or emergency rescue training in connection with service for Cal Fire, Sonoma County Volunteer Fire Department.

Approximate total employee count at Acme, Inc.: 75
Dates of training requested: September 8, 2026 through September 9, 2026
Days of training-leave already used this calendar year (if any): _______________
Name and location of training provider: _______________________________________________
Date this request is given to Acme, Inc.: _______________

RIGHT TO TRAINING LEAVE AT EMPLOYERS WITH 50 OR MORE EMPLOYEES
Under Labor Code § 230.4(a), an employee who performs duty as a volunteer firefighter, a reserve peace officer, or emergency rescue personnel, and who works for an employer employing 50 or more employees, must be permitted to take temporary leaves of absence, not to exceed an aggregate of 14 days per calendar year, for the purpose of engaging in fire, law enforcement, or emergency rescue training.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "230.4. (a) An employee who performs duty as a volunteer firefighter, a reserve peace officer, or as emergency rescue personnel, as defined in Section 230.3, and who works for an employer employing 50 or more employees, shall be permitted to take temporary leaves of absence, not to exceed an aggregate of 14 days per calendar year, for the purpose of engaging in fire, law enforcement, or emergency rescue training."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.4 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.4(a), training leave for employers with 50 or more employees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.4.)
  Known gap: This training-leave right is expressly limited to employers employing 50 or more employees; the verified text does not extend it to smaller employers, and this document does not independently address how "50 or more employees" is counted (for example, whether part-time employees, employees at affiliated entities, or a rolling headcount are counted), because the verified text of § 230.4 does not itself define that counting method. The 14-day figure is an aggregate annual cap across all training leave taken under this subdivision in a calendar year, not a per-training-event allowance, and the statute does not state whether this leave must be paid.

REMEDIES FOR VIOLATION OF THE TRAINING LEAVE RIGHT
An employee who works for an employer employing 50 or more employees, and who is discharged, threatened with discharge, demoted, suspended, or otherwise discriminated against in the terms and conditions of employment because the employee took time off for fire, law enforcement, or emergency rescue training under § 230.4(a), is entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the employer's acts.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(b) An employee who works for an employer employing 50 or more employees who is discharged, threatened with discharge, demoted, suspended, or in any other manner discriminated against in the terms and conditions of employment by his or her employer because the employee has taken time off to engage in fire, law enforcement, or emergency rescue training as provided in subdivision (a), is entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the acts of the employer."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.4 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.4(b), reinstatement and reimbursement remedy (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.4.)
  Known gap: Unlike the parallel emergency-duty remedy in § 230.3(b), § 230.4(b) does not itself contain a misdemeanor penalty for an employer's willful refusal to reinstate; this document does not assert that a comparable criminal penalty applies to a § 230.4 training-leave violation, because the verified text of § 230.4(b) does not state one. This remedy is available only to an employee at an employer employing 50 or more employees, consistent with the size-limited scope of the underlying right.

FILING A TRAINING-LEAVE COMPLAINT WITH THE LABOR COMMISSIONER
An employee seeking reinstatement and reimbursement under § 230.4 may file a complaint with the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement under Labor Code § 98.7, and upon receiving that type of complaint the Labor Commissioner proceeds as provided in § 98.7. Under § 98.7(a)(1), a person who believes they were discharged or otherwise discriminated against in violation of a law under the Labor Commissioner's jurisdiction may file a complaint with the division within one year after the violation occurred, and that one-year period may be extended for good cause.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(c) An employee seeking reinstatement and reimbursement pursuant to this section may file a complaint with the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement in accordance with Section 98.7 and, upon receipt of this type of complaint, the Labor Commissioner shall proceed as provided in that section."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.4 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.4(c), cross-reference to the Section 98.7 complaint procedure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.4.)
  "Any person who believes that they have been discharged or otherwise discriminated against in violation of any law under the jurisdiction of the Labor Commissioner may file a complaint with the division within one year after the occurrence of the violation. The one-year period may be extended for good cause."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 98.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 98.7(a)(1), one-year filing deadline and good-cause extension (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.7.)
  Known gap: Labor Code § 230.4(c) expressly cross-references the § 98.7 complaint procedure for a training-leave violation; § 230.3 does not contain the same cross-reference, so this document does not assert that the § 98.7 procedure is the exclusive or even an applicable route for an emergency-duty violation under § 230.3, only that it is the route the statute names for a training-leave violation under § 230.4. Section 98.7 itself is a general Labor Commissioner complaint procedure that applies to many Labor Code protections beyond this one, and this document does not describe those other uses; it covers only the one-year filing deadline and its good-cause extension, not the full investigation, hearing, injunctive-relief, and appeal procedures § 98.7 also establishes.
